item.title: Key U.S. Borrowing Rate Rises to Highest Level Since 2007
item.description:
The interest rate on a key U.S. government bond flirted with a nearly two-decade high, oil prices remained elevated and stock markets slipped on Tuesday amid intensifying turmoil in global markets.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury note briefly reached 5.04 percent, its highest since 2007, before easing back to around 5 percent. The yield flows through to higher rates on mortgages, business loans and other debt linked to government borrowing costs. Investors have shown increasing concerns about inflation and the direction of policy ahead of a Federal Reserve meeting to set interest rates, which concludes on Wednesday.

At the same time, the widening war in and around Iran is exacerbating worries about the flow of oil exports from the Middle East, putting upward pressure on oil, gasoline and diesel prices.

The price of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil, traded above $108 a barrel in choppy trade on Tuesday. The cost of crude has risen nearly 50 percent since the start of the war.

West Texas Intermediate crude, the U.S. benchmark, neared $106 a barrel, up about 58 percent since the start of the war.

Ship operators in the Persian Gulf remain wary of sending vessels through the Strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway between Iran and Oman. Over the past week, an average of about 20 ships passed through the strait, according to Kpler, a maritime data company. Before the war, about 130 ships a day and one-fifth of the world’s oil passed through the strait.

Advances by the Iranian-backed Houthi militia in Yemen have threatened oil shipments through the Red Sea, an alternative route to the Persian Gulf used by Saudi Arabia to get oil out to global markets. In addition, Saudi authorities have shut down the critical oil pipeline that shuttles oil from the Persian Gulf to the Red Sea, blaming a drone attack by an Iranian-backed Iraqi militia.

Crude prices eased after Chris Wright, the U.S. energy secretary, told CNBC on Tuesday that the shutdown was “a brief and temporary interruption,” and the Saudi pipeline would start operating again “very soon.” But prices began to rise again shortly after.

The 10-year Treasury yield, a crucial interest rate that influences many types of debt, rose on Tuesday to 5.04 percent, its highest level in nearly 20 years, before drifting back to around 5 percent. On Monday, this figure crossed 5 percent for only the second time since the global financial crisis. The 30-year yield, at 5.4 percent, has been trading at multidecade highs for the past several weeks.

In a recent survey of investment managers conducted by Deutsche Bank, the majority of respondents said worries about inflation were the most important factor pushing up bond yields, followed by uncertainty about Federal Reserve policy, the U.S. fiscal situation, the borrowing binge by artificial intelligence companies and other issues.

Wednesday will be a big day for the bond market. Traders expect Fed policymakers to announce an increase in their key interest rate at the end of their scheduled meeting, as inflation stubbornly runs above the central bank’s target and the economy remains resilient, in part because of enthusiastic spending by tech companies on A.I. systems.

Kevin Warsh, whose appointment as Fed chairman earlier this year was accompanied by demands from President Trump that he cut rates, faces a “simple choice,” according to analysts at Bank of America: “Hike or risk large bond spike.” If the Fed does not increase rates at its meeting this week, analysts say, bond traders could push long-term yields even higher as they doubt Mr. Warsh’s commitment to fighting inflation.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

The S&P 500 closed lower on Tuesday, extending Monday’s tech-driven losses. The benchmark index has fallen in five of the past six sessions.

In Europe, stocks fell. The Stoxx 600, a broad index that tracks the region’s largest companies, traded roughly flat for the day.

Stocks in Asia, where countries import vast quantities of oil and gas, were mostly down. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng and South Korea’s KOSPI both fell about 1 percent, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 was flat.

The average price of diesel rose to $6.27 per gallon on Tuesday, up 67 percent since the start of the war.

item.title: The Unlikely Political Bedfellows on A.I. Regulation
item.description:
Andrew here. In all of the back and forth over A.I. safety, a new concern has arisen. The chief technology officer of Palantir, Shyam Sankar, argues in an essay that the effective altruism movement is behind the freakout by A.I. researchers.

Sankar links effective altruism to Sam Bankman-Fried, the disgraced founder of FTX, who was an adherent. (It doesn’t explain the concerns of Elon Musk or Sam Altman, neither of whom is publicly tied to the philosophy; Dario Amodei has historical ties to the movement but says he’s not a member.) But this argument has been quietly swirling around Silicon Valley, especially among A.I. maximalists who favor less regulation and a need to compete against China. Remember that Palantir is a major military contractor.

Also: Our scoop on Monday about Jay Carney’s new job, working with Democrats on tech regulation, has caused quite a lot of discussion online. Barack Obama, whom Carney worked for as a press secretary, linked to a post featuring our newsletter. “Whether this technology results in amazing breakthroughs in medicine, energy and education or unleashes huge economic disruptions, greater inequality, and potential catastrophe will depend on the choices that we make right now — choices that should be made not just by the companies involved, but by all of us,” Obama wrote.

Opponents to potential new artificial intelligence regulation are getting more outspoken.

In one camp are those like President Trump, who see any slowdown as a weakening of U.S. national security. Another group is concerned with a different issue — and has drawn some unexpected allies.

Trump made clear that he opposes any sort of A.I. slowdown, further inserting himself into a debate over whether the technology is advancing at a dangerous pace.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT,” he wrote on social media on Monday.

He also derided Dario Amodei of Anthropic, who ignited the latest debate with a 3,800-word essay, as someone “now pretending to be a ‘perfect little angel.’”

“It’s a hoax,” Trump said on a phone call on Monday with Jensen Huang of Nvidia — while the billionaire C.E.O. was onstage at a conference.

Trump also reiterated his belief that the U.S. needed to maintain its lead over China, and argued that Beijing wasn’t seeking to restrain its A.I. industry. (That said, China’s spy chief argues that the technology could undermine the Chinese Communist Party’s hold on power and called for more regulation.)

Other skeptics of the A.I. industry’s latest call are making a different argument, one that has made strange bedfellows, including Lina Khan, the former F.T.C. chair who was frequently criticized by Silicon Valley executives for her approach to antitrust, and David Sacks, the investor and former Trump administration A.I. czar.

In an X post on Saturday, Khan argued that the government already had powerful tools to regulate A.I. companies:

Shipping flawed AI tools without implementing adequate measures to detect and stop rogue or defective AI agents can be an “unfair or deceptive” act or practice under the FTC Act (and analogous state laws). And some state AGs are already exploring holding AI firms and their CEOs criminally liable when their models participate in criminal activity.

Sacks told Bloomberg Television on Monday that he agreed with Khan, and dismissed A.I. companies’ requests for legal cover from antitrust laws to cooperate on safety standards. “You have a basic obligation to make your products safe,” he said. “Do not demand antitrust waivers or liability waivers in exchange for that.”

That said, Khan isn’t embracing his endorsement. In a statement to DealBook’s Niko Gallogly, she said:

While I’m glad to see a broad coalition for enforcing existing laws against these firms and their C.E.O.s, it is puzzling to see from people who’ve been cheering the dismantling of the administrative state and the corrupting of law enforcement. Who do they expect to do the work?

Sacks told DealBook in a statement:

I agree with Lina Khan that AI companies face massive product liability exposure if they release unsafe products, even without any new regulatory regimes. In my view, existing product liability laws are a good way to align the incentives of the major A.I. companies with safety objectives.

More on the politics of A.I. limits: On Tuesday, Steve Bannon, conservative commentator, and Senator Bernie Sanders, independent of Vermont, are set to speak at an event calling for stricter A.I. regulation.

And Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida, a Republican, argued that opposing greater regulation of A.I. was a “losing position” for his party in the midterms.

In other A.I. news: Microsoft published a provisional code of conduct for its A.I. models.

Oil rallies again. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, briefly surpassed $108 a barrel on Tuesday. A big fear is that a key Saudi Arabian pipeline could be offline for up to five weeks after a drone attack last week, The Associated Press reported, citing unnamed sources. Oil executives, including Mike Wirth of Chevron, are warning of a fuel crisis, contrasting with a rosier Trump administration outlook.

Cryptocurrencies slump before a key procedural congressional vote. Traders appear worried that the Clarity Act, a bill to regulate the crypto industry that President Trump supports, will fail to reach a crucial 60-vote threshold in the Senate on Tuesday. Bitcoin fell nearly 2 percent in choppy trading on Tuesday as Democrats remain largely opposed to the measure.

The Supreme Court rejects the Trump administration’s plan to restrict voting by mail. The ruling appears to draw a line under a weekslong legal tussle that voting rights groups and state officials worried could throw mail-in voting into chaos. But some observers are concerned that the overhaul efforts could still complicate the vote-collection process as Trump apparently seeks to cast doubt on the integrity of the vote in midterm elections.

The artificial intelligence boom has driven the nearly four-year bull market. But the prospect of an A.I. spending pullback is beginning to test investors’ nerves.

Wall Street is not saying that the A.I. rally is doomed. But worries about the technology, along with concerns about the war in Iran, inflation and potential rate hikes, have some analysts predicting more meager stock market gains ahead.

The latest:

The S&P 500 has fallen in five of the past six sessions, and the futures market this morning points to another tough open.

Shares in chipmakers, which have been a major beneficiary of the A.I. rally, were among the hardest hit on Monday after Dario Amodei of Anthropic and other industry leaders called for slowing development of the technology.

Enterprise software companies like Salesforce were some of the big winners on Monday. They had been considered especially vulnerable to disruption from A.I. models.

Brian Moynihan, the Bank of America C.E.O., warned on Monday of “relatively flat” trading revenues this quarter, a pronouncement that sank bank stocks.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury note briefly hit a multi-decade high this morning, pushing up borrowing costs for businesses and households.

What to watch: what Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has to say about the turmoil in the bond market — and the agency’s ineffective effort so far to calm it — when he testifies on Tueday before the House Committee on Financial Services.

Interest rates remain in focus, too. Trading this morning indicated a roughly 92 percent odds of the central bank raising its benchmark lending rate on Wednesday. That could put Kevin Warsh, the Fed chairman, in direct confrontation with President Trump, who reiterated over the weekend that the U.S. should have the world’s ​lowest interest rates.

The Fed may be the best suited to restore calm to the bond market, some analysts think. How? By raising rates to show the markets that it’s serious about fighting inflation.

What’s next? Investors will probably pore over the release on Wednesday of the Fed’s so-called dot plot projection on inflation and interest rates for clues about whether the central bank is gearing up for a series of rate increases.

That, too, could weigh on the A.I. trade.

quote of the day

Air Force Secretary Troy Meink, in the first public acknowledgment that the U.S. has stationed weapons in space. The statement drew consternation from Beijing: “We urge the U.S. side to stop expanding its military force and preparing for war in outer space,” Guo Jiakun, a spokesman for China’s Foreign Ministry, said at a regular news briefing on Tuesday.

Companies worried about protecting themselves from the threat of cyberattacks powered by artificial intelligence are now facing a conundrum. Cutting-edge A.I. models may provide the most powerful defense tools, but what if they take your data while guarding it?

That concern was underscored by a report published on Monday in The Information that Palantir Technologies, Booz Allen Hamilton and Nvidia are pulling back or restricting the use of Fable, the latest version of Anthropic’s Claude A.I. model.

But Rubrik, a cybersecurity company, is betting on the upside of harnessing the technology. On Tuesday, it announced Rubrik Code Guardian, a product that it developed with Anthropic, Sri Muppidi reports.

Some companies are wary of using Fable. That’s because it includes a 30-day data retention policy for “safety monitoring by default,” ostensibly to scan for breaches.

This has drawn pushback from Anthropic customers and partners, including Alex Karp of Palantir. “We were limited in our ability to actually roll out Fable,” said Eric Simons, the C.E.O. of StackBlitz, a coding platform that uses open-weight and closed-source models for its A.I. coding tool. That, he said, was because many of StackBlitz’s enterprise customers didn’t want it. The solution?

“You need zero data retention” for these models, Simons said.

Elsewhere, Rubrik sees an opportunity. The 12-year-old publicly traded company has a market value of more than $20 billion and specializes in backing up and recovering customer data.

How it works: Rubrik’s product creates a copy of customers’ code and identifies possible cyberattack vulnerabilities to developers using Anthropic’s Mythos model.

As more businesses adopt A.I., models and agents increasingly have access to sensitive corporate data. Code Guardian is intended to safeguard it, Bipul Sinha, Rubrik’s C.E.O., told DealBook.

Deals

Investors led by Michael Dell’s family office agreed to buy the Baldwin Group, an insurance broker, for $7.7 billion. (FT)

Kioxia, a Japanese memory chip maker, is said to be weighing a U.S. stock market listing that could raise at least $10 billion. (Bloomberg)

Politics, policy and regulation

The E.P.A. will end limits on emissions of coal- and gas-burning power plants, a move that could hamstring future administrations’ abilities to regulate the industry. (NYT)

The Treasury Department imposed sanctions on VTB Bank, a Russian lender, over its Iran ties. And France is lobbying E.U. countries to lift sanctions on the Uzbek Russian oligarch Alisher Usmanov. (CNBC, FT)

Best of the rest

“Ari Emanuel Tells the Inside Story of the Coup That Changed Hollywood Forever” (WSJ)

How Bob Kraft pushed the dropping of Macklemore from Ed Sheeran’s stadium tour over pro-Palestinian comments that the rapper made onstage. (NYT)

“Widow’s Bay,” its star, Matthew Rhys, and Apple were the big winners at the Emmy Awards last night. (NYT)

We’d like your feedback! Please email thoughts and suggestions to dealbook@nytimes.com.

]]>

item.title: Bessent Defends Faltering Bond Market Intervention
item.description:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended his intervention in the U.S. bond market on Tuesday, telling lawmakers that the decision to buy back American debt last week was successful, even as yields on 10-year Treasuries climbed higher in the wake of the purchases.

As Mr. Bessent testified before the House Financial Services Committee, the yield on the 10-year Treasury, which influences a wide range of borrowing costs, topped 5 percent and reached its highest level in 19 years.

Mr. Bessent suggested that bond yields might have crept even higher had he not intervened. He also sought to portray the Trump economy as delivering big gains to Americans, despite polls saying that voters are despondent about prices and the Iran war. Faced with repeated questions from Democrats about the high cost of living under President Trump, Mr. Bessent sought to blame inflation on the Biden administration even though Mr. Trump has been in office for nearly two years.

“I tell people I feel like an emergency room doctor for people who have been backed over by a truck,” Mr. Bessent said of the U.S. economy. “You had to stabilize the patient, and now the patient is up and able to walk and is going to get back on his or her feet.”

Mr. Bessent also echoed Mr. Trump’s promise to deliver a $5,000 dividend to Americans if Republicans retain control of Congress in the November midterm elections. The plan could add more than $1 trillion to the national debt and stoke inflation, but Mr. Bessent declined to offer details about where the money would come from or how it would help the economy at a moment when inflation remains elevated.

“I think putting more money in the American people’s pocket should be an objective for everyone, and I believe there are ways to do it that would not affect the deficit,” Mr. Bessent said.

When asked about whether such a plan would need the approval of Congress, Mr. Bessent said that the Treasury Department was studying that question and trying to determine where the money would come from.

“I’m not ready to discuss it at present, but at Treasury, we’ve been working on it for quite a while,” Mr. Bessent said.

The hearing, which turned tense at times, came as Mr. Bessent has been in the spotlight for intervening in financial markets in an effort to lower interest rates. The Treasury secretary acknowledged on Tuesday that the recent rise in yields reflects concerns about U.S. deficits, but he offered no plan for how to address them.

“We will be talking about a fiscal consolidation plan that is coming,” Mr. Bessent said, referring to a forthcoming government initiative to cut spending that he first referenced last month.

Mr. Bessent’s ambitions of spurring economic growth and reducing deficits have been undercut by Mr. Trump’s decision to start a war with Iran. The conflict has sent energy prices rising around the world, stoking inflation and forcing the U.S. to beef up military spending.

The Treasury secretary, who was heckled by protesters opposing the Iran war, sparred with lawmakers for three hours. When pressed by Democrats, he expressed doubts about their data, questioned their intelligence and said that signs of economic malaise were the results of former President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s policies.

“Can I ask what’s the statute of limitations on the Joe Biden blame game?” Representative Ritchie Torres, Democrat of New York, asked. “Like when in doubt, blame Joe Biden. Is that the modus operandi of this administration?”

item.title: With Emmys Haul, Apple Joins the Big Leagues of TV
item.description:
After “Widow’s Bay” took best comedy honors at the Emmy Awards on Monday night, the show’s creator, Katie Dippold, grabbed her statuette and paid tribute to “the wonderful weirdos” who worked on the show. She then quickly switched gears because she had a tech colossus to thank: Apple.

“They truly just let us do this weird show,” she said from the Emmys stage.

It was a big win for “Widow’s Bay,” a horror-comedy about the oddball inhabitants of a haunted New England island. The show, which stars Matthew Rhys, was lauded by Emmy voters for being a distinctly original series in a television landscape that relies a bit too much on old ideas and recycled intellectual property.

The victory also cemented Apple’s now-critical place in the entertainment industry.

Fueled by “Widow’s Bay,” which set a record for most Emmy wins for a comedy series, with 14, as well as sci-fi series “Pluribus” and “Slow Horses,” Apple broke a long-running streak on Monday night. Since 2003, HBO, Netflix and FX have been the only outlets to claim bragging rights on Emmys night. Apple’s 28 awards this year easily outpaced all three.

Apple’s entry into Hollywood less than a decade ago — the company started buying projects in 2017, and debuted its streaming service in 2019 — was greeted with skepticism. Other technology companies, including Microsoft, Facebook and Yahoo, had also started making scripted TV series before quickly fleeing town. Becoming an entertainment studio is as expensive as finding hits is a slow, unpredictable and frustrating process.

While Apple TV remains little watched compared with its competitors, the company has stuck with it.

“When we started this seven years ago, it’s hard to imagine that we’d be here today,” said Eddy Cue, a top Apple executive who started the entertainment division and hired the company’s lead Hollywood executives, Zack Van Amburg and Jamie Erlicht.

Mr. Cue was speaking at the Emmys official after party shortly after he led a triumphant, fist-raising tequila-shot toast to his colleagues.

One of the people in the toast circle was Apple’s new chief executive, John Ternus. Many in Hollywood have been anxious that Apple’s foray into entertainment — seemingly not a core business interest — could be curtailed when Mr. Ternus, the company’s head of hardware engineering, took over from Tim Cook. But his presence at the ceremony suggested otherwise.

“At Apple, we always focus on the customer, build the best thing that we can on the product side, and the Apple TV team is doing the exact same thing with TV shows,” Mr. Ternus said during an interview at the after party.

He added: “Seven years to have done all of this is extraordinary, but we’re just getting started.”

Since 2022, nearly every media company has drastically cut back on spending. The era of Peak TV is over; the number of Emmy-eligible dramas, comedies and limited series this year, 212, declined 39 percent from four years ago.

But Apple, often looking for projects with big stars and bigger budgets, is still spending. “At a time of profound change in our business, their willingness to think long-term and invest in artists really stands out,” said Richard Weitz, a co-chairman of the WME Group, which includes one of the major talent agencies in Hollywood.

He continued: “They’re serious, they’re spending money and they’re making a lot of programming — they’ve become absolutely critical to our marketplace.”

This is not the first time Apple has proved popular with award voters. It won best picture at the 2022 Oscars with “Coda” and took best comedy at the Emmys three times before — twice with “Ted Lasso” and last year with “The Studio.”

The company’s streaming service, which, unlike Netflix and Disney, doesn’t have a library of old movies and TV series, is still not widely watched, however. In July, it made up 0.5 percent of all TV viewing time, a fraction of its competitors’, according to Nielsen. Netflix attracted nearly 8 percent of all viewing time in the United States, Disney’s streaming services came in at close to 5 percent, and free streaming services like Roku and Tubi also had more viewership.

Though Apple’s top hits, like “Ted Lasso” and “Severance,” draw big audiences, the shows that won big at the Emmys struggled to find viewers. “Widow’s Bay” was the least watched of all the best comedy nominees, Nielsen said. In the drama category, Apple’s three entrants — “Pluribus,” “Your Friends & Neighbors,” and “Slow Horses” — ranked among the least-watched drama series nominees, and were dwarfed by one of the biggest hits in television, “The Pitt” on HBO Max.

“The Pitt,” which took best drama honors for the second year in a row, helped HBO Max finish second on Emmy night, with 21 awards. “DTF St. Louis” won best limited series, and Jean Smart, the star of “Hacks,” tied Cloris Leachman and Julia Louis-Dreyfus for most acting Emmy wins ever (eight).

For the moment, though, Apple TV has passed Netflix when it comes to making prestige television. Netflix won just 16 Emmys this year, its lowest output since 2016 when the company produced fewer programs than it does now.

Back at the Emmys after party, Mr. Cue was taking it all in.

“We want to create the best shows on television,” he said. “We want them to be about quality. We want to make people cry. We want people to laugh. We want to make people think.”

He added: “I’m pinching myself, honestly.”

item.title: Chinese Firms Used Binance to Launder Iranian Oil Money, Prosecutors Say
item.description:
Two Chinese companies used accounts on the cryptocurrency exchange Binance to launder illegal proceeds from the sale of Iranian oil, the Justice Department said in court papers.

In a civil forfeiture claim filed in federal court in Manhattan on Monday, prosecutors said that the two companies had moved funds intended to finance the Iranian military, including the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, which the United States has classified as a terrorist organization. Binance was not charged with any wrongdoing.

A group of crypto wallets linked to Iran received more than $1.5 billion of the illegal proceeds, the complaint said, though it wasn’t clear exactly how much of that money had moved through Binance, the world’s largest crypto trading platform. The Justice Department plans to seize $61 million, currently held in a set of accounts overseen by Tether, another crypto firm, the complaint said.

The flow of illicit funds through Binance was flagged internally last year by a group of the exchange’s compliance officials, according to reports in The New York Times and other outlets. Binance fired or suspended the officials after they pointed out the Iran transactions; the company said the discipline had nothing to do with their warnings.

The reports in The Times raised concerns in Congress, where a top Senate Democrat opened an investigation into Binance. For years, the company has struggled to eliminate financial crime on its platform. It paid $4.3 billion in penalties in 2023 after pleading guilty to violating U.S. financial laws.

A Binance spokeswoman said in a statement that the exchange had “zero tolerance for sanctions violations or illicit activity.”

“This case was not filed against Binance and does not allege wrongdoing by Binance,” she said. “Binance did not permit any transactions with sanctioned individuals.”

Got a confidential news tip? The New York Times would like to hear from readers who want to share messages and materials with our journalists.

Binance has tried to stop illegal activity on its platform since the 2023 settlement, pledging to work with law enforcement around the world to root out financial crime. Its founder, Changpeng Zhao, stepped down as chief executive and served four months in prison.

Last year, Binance forged a business relationship with World Liberty Financial, the crypto start-up founded by President Trump and his three sons. Mr. Trump granted Mr. Zhao a pardon in October.

Around that time, the compliance officials at Binance raised internal alarms over the movement of funds to Iran, identifying the same two companies named in the complaint. One, Hexa Whale, a firm based in Hong Kong, used Binance to send $490 million to crypto wallets tied to Iranian entities, the employees reported. They found that another $1.2 billion had flowed to Iran-linked entities from an account owned by the financial firm Blessed Trust, a Binance business partner in Hong Kong.

The Binance investigators also learned that an account belonging to Blessed Trust’s chief executive and one controlled by a group of Binance employees had both been accessed from the same electronic device. In the exchange’s internal systems, accounts belonging to Blessed Trust and its chief executive were marked with a note: “Don’t block. Internal accounts,” The Times reported in March.

Binance has disputed many of the employees’ findings. The company said this year that Blessed Trust was “one of several vendors for Binance” and that the exchange did not control it. Blessed Trust did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Hexa Whale has ceased operations.

In the court filing on Monday, the Justice Department said that Blessed Trust and Hexa Whale had used Binance to launder the proceeds from black market sales of Iranian oil to buyers in China. The money was funneled to the Iranian government, the complaint said, and used to finance “terrorist activities,” a violation of U.S. sanctions.

Blessed Trust misrepresented to crypto and financial firms that it provided “wealth management” and other seemingly legitimate services, the complaint said.

“Today’s action demonstrates our determination to deprive the Government of Iran and its terrorist proxies of the illegal money they rely on,” Deputy U.S. Attorney Sean S. Buckley said in a statement. “The Government of Iran relies on black-market sales of sanctioned crude oil to fund its military and foster terrorism in the Middle East and around the world.”

item.title: The New Restaurant at the Public Theater Revives the Astor Family Name
item.description:
The former Library, the second-floor dining room run by Andrew Carmellini and his NoHo Hospitality Group in the Public Theater, has a new identity. Named for the founding family of the building, which once housed a library and has been home to the theater since 1967, the space has been refreshed. Woven into a custom carpet by Paula Scher are the names of the theater’s productions, and a mural by Andre Carillho at the bar shows writers and Public Theater celebrities, like Joe Papp. Casual, sometimes clever food like pigs in Wellington and a French dip with mushrooms enliven the menu. On the ground floor below, the new tambour-paneled Bar Torino along one wall, open from 10 a.m., starts with panini and pastries, then pairs Italian snacks with aperitivi.

The Public Theater, 425 Lafayette Street (Astor Place), 212-539-8777, theastornyc.com.

At Lana Lagomarsini’s new spot, the Bravo Top Chef contender’s first, the format is a tasting menu, for 12 at a time, with multiple seatings each night. Her food draws alluringly on the African diaspora through the Caribbean, the American South and family history with dishes like oxtail pâté en croûte, scallops with white barbecue sauce, trout in collard green potlikker consommé, elk with blackberry jerk and passion fruit tiramisù. Blue velvet banquettes add polish to the compact setting.

1261 Park Avenue (97th Street), creolanyc.com.

Catch Hospitality Group’s portfolio keeps growing. Having opened the Corner Store, the Eighty Six and Or’esh, Eugene Remm and his partners are now tapping the Mediterranean as it laps the Côte d’Azur. Bistro specialties in what’s billed as a coastal brasserie provide a somewhat muddled approach and it’s up to the executive chef Jake Tyler Brodsky, who worked at Eleven Madison Park, to sort it out. It’s French. Steak frites anchors the menu.

340 Bleecker Street (West 10th Street), 212-308-3408, cafecharmantnyc.com.

In the brick-walled Upper East Side space that had been Bayon, Korean fare has replaced Cambodian. It’s a welcome addition to the neighborhood, with a menu that skews traditional. Expect dumplings, banchan, japchae, bibimbap, short-rib soup, pancakes and spicy pork bulgogi. A backyard garden should add to the allure.

408 East 64th Street.

Boutique food markets are becoming as essential as nail salons to New York neighborhoods. Austin Johnson, who was the chef and founder at One White Street and its adjacent Rigor Hill Market, has left those TriBeCa spots to create this market, named for the Hudson Valley, and then some in the West Village. With his partner, Eytan Sugarman of the White Horse Tavern across the street, he has folded a bakery; a source for local produce; a butcher cutting oven-ready meats; and a roster of prepared food from early breakfast sandwiches to rotisserie chickens, potpies and more, including pet food, into this fairly generous space. (Friday)

569 Hudson Street (Bank Street), 646-898-8210, hvalleynyc.com.

Works & Process, the showcase for new works in performing arts for more than 40 years, is offering dinner-theater next month at Free Food Refettorio Harlem, which provides support and meals for those in need. On Oct. 2, 7, 16 and 21, from 5:15 to 6:45 p.m., there will be a dinner prepared and served by volunteers with a performance from 5:45 to 6 p.m. of the 24/7 Diner by Master Z at Work Dance Family with Courtney Washington, who goes by Balenciaga. The commissioned work is about an all-night diner. The evening is free, first-come, first-served, and open to the public (there are 120 seats each night).

37 West 119th Street, worksandprocess.org.

This former head chef at Sushi of Gari is now a member of the culinary team at Sushi Koju in the Ace Hotel in Downtown Brooklyn. He is working with chefs Tetsuro Otomo and Sho Boo. Kevin Garrison, the former executive chef of this Brooklyn Sushi Koju, is off to Miami to open a branch there.

Mr. Luca is the new executive chef at Ginger Ristorante, an import from Rome near Rockefeller Center. He’s joined by Ms. Gomez, the new pastry chef.

Jake Dickson has expanded his territory on the lower level of Chelsea Market to include fresh produce, mostly local. and organic, and some groceries and salads, in addition to his usual meats, poultry and prepared foods. He’s aiming to fill the gap left by the closing of Manhattan Fruit Market in the market. His approach pointedly avoids competing with other vendors so you’ll find Pickle Guys products but no cheeses, for example. (Wednesday)

75 Ninth Avenue (15th Street), dicksonsfarmstand.com.

A Little Italy staple for more than 130 years, until it closed in 2023, has reopened on the main level of Chelsea Market. Sandwiches, cannolis, cheeses and cured meats stock the new outlet.

75 Ninth Avenue (15th Street), allevadairy.com.

Chile crisp has nothing to worry about. But this relish from Jim Pileski, who served it at his now-closed Long Island City, Queens, restaurant, Burger Garage, provides a suitably zesty finish to a burger, a hot dog or a taco. Chopped roasted jalapeños in soy sauce with a little citric acid are all that’s in the dark, moderately hot, briny condiment that Mr. Pileski is now having produced. Stir some into guacamole, add it to the sour cream on a baked potato or let it ignite those huevos. It’s high-end at $19.95 plus shipping, but a little goes a long way.

item.title: Poverty Rate Was Stable Before Trump’s Safety Net Cuts Gained Force
item.description:
The financial well-being of Americans held relatively steady last year, even as the cost of living continued to climb.

The poverty rate was 13.1 percent in 2025, the same as in 2024, according to data released on Tuesday by the Census Bureau. Poverty for children and people over age 65 did not change, while poverty among those without a high school degree rose. The share of Americans without health insurance stayed level.

Median household income improved last year to $87,460, the highest level on record, adjusted for inflation. But Americans remain highly anxious about their ability to pay for groceries, housing, child care, and other goods and services. Inflation remains elevated, eroding workers’ paychecks. Higher gas prices brought on by the war in Iran are further straining household budgets.

The poverty data does not capture many of the changes enacted in the sweeping Republican domestic policy bill passed in July 2025, including substantial cuts to Medicaid, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and other government aid. Analysts and advocates for those programs anticipate that the effect of reductions to the country’s social safety net will become more visible in the reports that cover 2026, 2027 and beyond.

“In many ways, 2025 represents a base line from which we’ll see bigger cuts in the years after,” said Gideon Lukens, a senior fellow and the director of research and data analysis at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. “It’s the calm before the storm.”

Many of the safety net programs that are facing steep cuts prevented people from falling into hardship last year. Refundable tax credits, including the earned-income tax credit and the child tax credit, shielded 6.1 million people from poverty in 2025. SNAP benefits lifted 3.1 million people out of poverty. On the flip side, medical expenses drove 7.7 million people into poverty, a number that could increase in the coming years because more Americans are expected to lose health coverage as a result of legislative changes.

For Alicia Quirk, 30, federal programs including Medicaid and food stamps have been instrumental in keeping her family afloat. She and her husband, who have three young children, used to make $100,000 a year as corrections officers at the county jail. But she stopped working three years ago to care for her son, who struggles to keep his oxygen levels up and has autism and epilepsy. Her husband, seeking a more predictable work schedule, now works in construction making $25 an hour.

His wages, along with her occasional stints delivering for DoorDash and Instacart, are generally enough for necessities and items for her children, though she sometimes forgoes paying rent or utility bills when things get tight. Still, she was dismayed and confused when she received a letter recently informing her that she was losing her food stamp benefits because her family’s income exceeded the eligibility limit. Her husband’s construction job is temporarily paused, so he is not bringing in any income.

“Everyone still has to eat, and everyone still needs all these things,” she said.

The Census reports are considered the most complete accounts of the nation’s rates of poverty and health insurance coverage, but the data lags. The reports for 2026 will not come out for another year.

The official poverty rate, which is considered to be an outdated measurement because it does not take into account many of the government’s anti-poverty programs, ticked down slightly to 10.2 percent from 10.7 in 2024.

The data reflected the low unemployment, solid wage growth and strong hiring in health care and related professions that characterized the job market last year.

Median earnings for women working full time increased 3.2 percent and stayed flat for men, which drove the ratio between female and male earnings up to 83.9 percent and reversed two years of declines.

Steven Durlauf, the director of the Stone Center for Research on Wealth Inequality and Mobility at the University of Chicago, said that divergence aligned with shifting dynamics in the labor market, including the decline in labor force participation for men.

“These numbers are reflecting the compositional changes in jobs that emerged over the last year,” he said.

The fairly stable headline numbers in the reports mask some concerning signs below the surface.

The supplemental poverty rate for people 65 and older, for instance, climbed to 15.4 percent last year from 9.4 percent in 2020.

The Ohio Association of Foodbanks has seen demand for its food services increase since the pandemic, partly because older Ohioans who often have set incomes are having more trouble adjusting to rising costs, said Joree Novotny, the organization’s executive director.

“Those fixed incomes aren’t able to stretch and keep up with much higher-than-average rates of increases of basic necessities,” she said.

She is worried that the Trump administration’s new rules restricting food stamp eligibility could make it even more difficult for Ohioans to feed themselves.

The data also revealed that income inequality persisted last year. The wealthiest households saw their income increase 1.7 percent, while the poorest households effectively experienced no change in their income.

“The people who are feeling the inflation impact are people who are lowest income,” said Wendy Chun-Hoon, the president of the left-leaning Center for Law and Social Policy.

Overall, the share of Americans who lack health insurance did not change much. The uninsured rate was 7.9 percent in 2025, similar to 2024. But the uninsured rate has very likely risen higher this year. The expiration of tax credits that helped many Americans buy health insurance in Obamacare marketplaces has driven a drop in enrollment by several million people.

Legislative changes to SNAP have also caused reductions in enrollment. Nationwide, enrollment in the food assistance program has fallen, with particularly drastic reductions in a handful of states.

The tax and domestic policy bill the Republican Congress passed last year will also bring changes to health care programs next year that are expected to further increase the uninsured population. The law added a new work requirement for childless adults in Medicaid and restrictions on coverage in several public programs for legal immigrants. The Congressional Budget Office estimates around 10 million more people will be uninsured in 2034 as a result of the legislation.

item.title: Senate Votes to Block Crypto Bill in Major Blow to the Industry
item.description:
A sweeping bill that would create business-friendly rules for cryptocurrencies stalled in the Senate on Tuesday, a major blow to the crypto industry’s plans in Washington.

The Senate voted 50 to 49 to block consideration of the Clarity Act, a high-profile piece of legislation that was shaped by crypto executives over months of negotiations with Congress and the White House. The bill passed in the House last year, but it has faced numerous delays in the Senate.

The vote on Tuesday was a stinging defeat for the industry that makes it unlikely the legislation will pass anytime soon — if ever. With the midterm elections coming up in November, the window to advance it is closing rapidly, despite more than $100 million in political spending by crypto companies.

While many Republicans embraced the bill, Democrats largely opposed it. Many of their concerns centered on President Trump, who generated $1.4 billion from a network of crypto businesses last year. Democrats wanted stronger language to prevent the president and other public officials from using crypto to make money.

Ultimately, no Democrat voted for the bill, leaving Republicans well short of the 60-vote threshold required to proceed. Several Republicans, including Senator Susan Collins of Maine and Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri, also cast “no” votes.

“All President Trump wants is for the Senate to give him time to crime, and I won’t support any piece of legislation that enables him,” Senator Ruben Gallego, Democrat of Arizona, said in a statement after the vote. “This legislation failed squarely because Republicans refuse to say no to the president.”

The outcome was a bitter disappointment for crypto executives, who had made the Clarity Act their most important policy priority.

“Today’s vote was a failure of leadership,” Mason Lynaugh, executive director of the Stand With Crypto advocacy group, said in a statement. “Every day without action is a day that American innovation, jobs, and investments continue to be shipped overseas.”

Under the Biden administration, U.S. financial regulators cracked down on the crypto industry, filing lawsuits against top companies including Coinbase and Kraken. They argued that digital currencies were subject to the same strict rules as securities, like the stocks and bonds traded on Wall Street.

The industry was outraged and spent more than $130 million to fight back, funding a network of super PACs that helped elect pro-crypto legislators in the 2024 election.

When he took office, Mr. Trump ended the regulatory crackdown on crypto companies. But the industry wanted more — a bill that would enshrine his pro-industry position into law. If the Clarity Act had passed, crypto executives wouldn’t have had to worry about a future administration reviving the Biden administration’s aggressive legal strategy.

The bill passed the House with a bipartisan vote in July 2025. But the Senate has proved harder to navigate. For much of this year, the influential banking lobby argued that the bill would hurt banks by redirecting traditional deposits into crypto, causing concern among some Republicans.

But the focus of the recent debate has been Mr. Trump’s crypto profits. This week, Republicans released new language to address ethics concerns, including a provision that would bar federal officials from issuing or sponsoring digital coins. The new language also gave state attorneys general a role in enforcing the ethics rules — addressing a demand that Democrats made during a previous round of debate.

Democrats were not satisfied, arguing that the language was full of loopholes. Senator Richard Blumenthal, Democrat of Connecticut, called the rules a “charade” and a “sham.”

“The president’s latest attempt to write his own crypto ethics bill leaves wide loopholes, giving himself time to restructure his crypto venture companies so that he can continue to draw down unprecedented profits,” Virginia Canter of Democracy Defenders Action, an advocacy group, said in a statement.

The crypto industry still has major funds at its disposal. As of the beginning of August, a network of pro-crypto super PACs had about $123 million on hand, which it could spend to boost the industry’s favored candidates in the midterms or oppose crypto skeptics.

The industry has already secured major victories under Mr. Trump. Last year, Congress passed the Genius Act, creating industry-friendly rules for a type of cryptocurrency known as a stablecoin. And regulatory agencies like the Securities and Exchange Commission have adopted favorable policies toward crypto.

The vote on Tuesday was “a real setback, but it does not take away from all of the progress that has already been made under this pro-crypto administration,” said Joseph Chalom, the chief executive of the crypto firm Sharplink.

Michael Gold and Theodore Schleifer contributed reporting.

item.title: Data Center’s Spill of 5,000 Gallons of Diesel Forces N.J. River Cleanup
item.description:
Cleanup is underway near the Hackensack River in New Jersey where about 5,000 gallons of fuel spilled from a data center, state officials said. The spill renewed fears of the environmental dangers linked to the expanding use of A.I. systems.

The diesel fuel began leaking from a storage tank at an Equinix data center in Secaucus, N.J., on Friday night, the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection said in a statement on Tuesday.

The spill is now contained, the agency said, adding that “a significant portion of the fuel” was removed from over the weekend.

The creek meanders through an industrial park and enters the Hackensack River. The agency said the fuel was contained before it reached the river itself. Crews are expected to be on the site for several days.

The agency and the U.S. Coast Guard have been monitoring the river and protective booms placed at the mouth of the creek “and have not observed impacts to the river or to wildlife,” the statement said.

Equinix said in a statement that it was “conducting a full investigation to determine the root cause and prevent recurrence” at the data center, which sits less than four miles from Manhattan. It has also brought in an environmental remediation company.

According to Equinix’s website, the data center in question “serves the world’s largest financial, media and enterprise companies” and is about 130,000 square feet. It is one of four Equinix data centers in Secaucus.

Michael Gonnelli, the mayor of Secaucus, told News 12 New Jersey that the spill was a result of a “computer glitch.”

In a statement on Monday, Mr. Gonnelli said the spill “should never have happened.”

Crews worked over the weekend and have cleaned up about 3,500 gallons, so far, he said.

Data centers have become a political flashpoint as many voters worry about the health and environmental, existential and economic effects of artificial intelligence.

The centers use large amounts of electricity and require large amounts of cold water to cool equipment. For nearby residents and businesses, this can translate into soaring energy bills and an increased strain on the electric grid.

The potential risk of power outages leads many data centers to rely on backup power generators, which typically run on diesel fuel.

In 2024, the diesel generator capacity at data centers across the country nearly tripled, according to a report by the Better Data Center Project, an advocacy group. As many data centers are near bodies of water, the risk of fuel spilling into the water increases with the amount of diesel stored on site.

The issue is especially pronounced in states that host very large data centers, such as Virginia, where more than 10,500 generator units — 99 percent of which are powered by diesel — had received permits by late 2025, the report said. Many large, or hyper-scale, data centers can have multiple diesel generators the size of train cars at a single site, the report said.

In addition to emergencies, generators can also be used when there is a minor disturbance in electricity services, or when businesses are asked to conserve energy during heat waves. Generators also must be run regularly for testing and maintenance.

At a town hall meeting this summer in Orangetown, N.Y., about 30 miles north of New York City, about a proposed data center expansion in the area, residents complained of noise, light and air pollution resulting from routine generator maintenance.

Diesel spills are rare, and when they occur they are relatively small, according to the Better Data Center Project report.

But the effects of spills can persist. In 2008, a 15,000 gallon leak in Washington state required groundwater monitoring for over a decade.

The data center spill in Secaucus was not New Jersey’s first, according to the Better Data Center Project; in 2017, a 600-gallon leak in Clifton affected the region’s storm drains.

Many activists cited the Secaucus spill as evidence that Gov. Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey should institute a statewide moratorium on data centers. So far, the governor has implemented some statewide regulatory guardrails but has left zoning decisions to individual towns.

“Data centers create problems that don’t stop at municipal boundaries,” said Ben Dziobek, the executive director of Climate Revolution Action Network, a nonprofit. Even though Jersey City and Bayonne had banned data centers, he said, they still lived with the risk of pollution from spills like the one in Secaucus.

Stephen Sigmund, Gov. Sherrill’s spokesman, said that New Jersey had “the most comprehensive data center plan in the nation” and that it “put power back in the hands of local communities” to keep data centers accountable for environmental damage.

item.title: Debut of Bari Weiss’s ‘60 Minutes’ Sees Dip in the Ratings
item.description:
After a chaotic off-season, “60 Minutes” returned to CBS on Sunday with a revamped show, a buzzy publicity campaign and an exclusive interview with an Air Force pilot shot down over Iran.

All the commotion did not translate into a ratings success.

Viewership for the season premiere of “60 Minutes” fell roughly 21 percent from a year ago, according to Nielsen, making it the lowest-rated premiere of the long-running show in recent memory.

The Nielsen number — 7.9 million viewers in total, down from 10 million last year — is a disquieting result for Bari Weiss, CBS’s editor in chief, whose overhaul of “60 Minutes” has become an early test of her tenure.

Ms. Weiss purged the show’s senior leadership, fired several correspondents and installed a new executive producer, Nick Bilton, who promised a modernization.

Critics of Ms. Weiss were quick to attribute Sunday’s decline in ratings to her decision-making. But television ratings are contingent on many factors.

In most of the country, “60 Minutes” airs immediately after National Football League games, and ratings often fluctuate depending on the matchup that precedes the show. Ahead of last year’s premiere, CBS had the N.F.L.’s marquee late-afternoon game to itself; this past Sunday, CBS and Fox both aired games that kicked off at the same time.

That competition contributed to a drop in viewership for CBS’s late-afternoon football, which drew about 22 percent fewer viewers than a year ago.

Still, the novelty factor of a revised “60 Minutes” — especially after extensive coverage of behind-the-scenes drama at the show, including the firing of Scott Pelley — had raised expectations that curious viewers would tune in. CBS invested in an extensive marketing campaign, including billboards in Times Square that urged onlookers “to see for yourself” before judging the show.

CBS News said in a statement on Tuesday: “We are so proud of the exceptional journalism on display in our season premiere and we can’t wait to bring our audience another amazing show this coming Sunday.”

“60 Minutes” remains the most popular news program on television, and last season it averaged 9.1 million viewers an episode, up 9 percent from the year before. In recent years, viewership for the season premiere has typically ranged from just below 10 million to just below 12 million people.

That past success fueled questions about why Ms. Weiss had decided to overhaul what was arguably the strongest franchise in the CBS News portfolio.

Yet for all the hype, Sunday’s episode looked a lot like previous editions of the show.

Norah O’Donnell interviewed the Air Force colonel about his rescue from Iran. Lesley Stahl investigated the underground economy that has developed around President Trump’s liberal use of pardons. L. Jon Wertheim profiled the coach of the Los Angeles Rams, Sean McVay.

Mr. Bilton, a technology journalist and filmmaker, made some graphical enhancements, like a sleeker-looking stopwatch during the show’s signature “tick, tick, tick” introduction. The program also deployed a hidden camera for the Stahl segment, reviving a “60 Minutes” technique that had fallen out of favor in recent years.

item.title: OpenAI Considers New Financing at a $1.5 Trillion Valuation
item.description:
OpenAI is considering a new funding round that would value the giant artificial intelligence start-up at about $1.5 trillion in advance of its planned initial public offering, according to people familiar with the matter.

If successful, it would roughly double OpenAI’s most recent private valuation of $730 billion, crowning the ChatGPT maker as the world’s most valuable privately held company.

The people familiar with the discussions, who requested anonymity to share details of the potential financing, stressed that no decisions had been made and that plans may change.

Investors recently approached OpenAI with a proposal to invest in the start-up at a $1.2 trillion valuation, according to the people. But OpenAI believes it should be given a value of at least $1.5 trillion based on increased customer traction with its coding tool Codex and its latest A.I. models, GPT-6 Astra and GPT-5.6 Sol, according to the people.

OpenAI generated more than $40 billion in annualized revenue last month, roughly double its sales figure at the end of last year.

The ChatGPT maker expects to go public next year. OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, has said that the company delayed its I.P.O. to focus on safety risks from A.I., though the company had already shelved its plan for a 2026 public offering to shore up its finances.

One consideration for OpenAI as it considers the new round of financing is that the start-up already confidentially filed its draft prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June. It will need to carefully navigate securities laws when sharing confidential information with investors.

OpenAI has raised more than $180 billion since its founding in 2015. In its most recent round, the company brought in a record $122 billion at a $730 billion valuation before adding the new capital raised.

Its rival, Anthropic, is making preparations to go public this fall in what could be the world’s largest public offering. The start-up, whose chief executive is Dario Amodei, could raise more than $100 billion at a $2 trillion valuation. Anthropic’s business has surged ahead of OpenAI recently, with the start-up increasing its annualized revenue to roughly $65 billion at the end of the second quarter.

The Financial Times previously reported some details of the company’s potential fund-raising.
